field_operations.original: [L2] A Euclidean $C^1$ map with invertible derivative at a point has a local $C^1$ inverse ([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]).
field_operations.proposed: [L2] In dimension $n\ge1$, a Euclidean $C^1$ map with invertible derivative at a point has a local $C^1$ inverse ([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]).

field_operations.original: [L4] Chart maps and their inverses are smooth diffeomorphisms onto open Euclidean sets ([[prop-chart-maps-are-diffeomorphisms-onto-euclidean-open-sets]]).
field_operations.proposed:
[L4] Chart maps and their inverses are smooth diffeomorphisms onto open Euclidean sets ([[prop-chart-maps-are-diffeomorphisms-onto-euclidean-open-sets]]).

[L5] The tangent space of a smooth $n$-manifold has dimension $n$, including $n=0$ ([[cor-the-tangent-space-of-an-n-manifold-has-dimension-n]]).

[L6] A smooth map is continuous and has smooth coordinate representatives on compatible chart neighbourhoods; maps on open subsets of $\mathbb R^0$ are declared smooth ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]).

field_operations.original: 1.1 Choose smooth charts $(U_0,\varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V_0,\psi)$ at $F(p)$ as in [L4], and let $f:=\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}$. By [L4], the chart maps $\varphi^{-1}$ and $\psi$ are diffeomorphisms, so their differentials are linear isomorphisms. Applying [L1] gives $$ D f(\varphi(p))=d\psi_{F(p)}\circ dF_p\circ d(\varphi^{-1})_{\varphi(p)}. $$ Because $dF_p$ is an isomorphism by [F1], the Euclidean differential $D f(\varphi(p))$ is invertible. [F1, L1, L4, given]
field_operations.proposed:
1.1 By [L5], the isomorphism $dF_p$ implies that $M$ and $N$ have the same dimension $n$. If $n=0$, smooth charts at $p$ and $F(p)$ have nonempty open images in the singleton $\mathbb R^0$, so their domains are the open singletons $U=\{p\}$ and $V=\{F(p)\}$. The restriction $F|_U:U\to V$ is bijective, and its inverse has the unique map $\mathbb R^0\to\mathbb R^0$ as its coordinate representative, which is smooth by [L6]. Thus the conclusion holds when $n=0$. For the remainder assume $n\ge1$. [L4, L5, L6, given, cases, algebra]

1.2 Choose smooth charts $(U_0,\varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V_0,\psi)$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, as permitted by smoothness in [L6], and let $f:=\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}$. By [L4], the chart maps $\varphi^{-1}$ and $\psi$ are diffeomorphisms, so their differentials are linear isomorphisms. Applying [L1] gives $$ D f(\varphi(p))=d\psi_{F(p)}\circ dF_p\circ d(\varphi^{-1})_{\varphi(p)}. $$ Because $dF_p$ is an isomorphism by [F1], the Euclidean differential $D f(\varphi(p))$ is invertible. [F1, L1, L4, L6, given]

field_operations.original: 2.1 By [L2], after shrinking to open neighbourhoods $\widetilde U\subseteq\varphi(U_0)$ and $\widetilde V\subseteq\psi(V_0)$ of $\varphi(p)$ and $\psi(F(p))$, the restriction $f|\widetilde U:\widetilde U\to \widetilde V$ is a bijection with $C^1$ inverse. Since $f$ is smooth, [L3] upgrades that inverse to a smooth one. [step 1.1, L2, L3]
field_operations.proposed: 2.1 Since $n\ge1$, [L2] applies: after shrinking to open neighbourhoods $\widetilde U\subseteq\varphi(U_0)$ and $\widetilde V\subseteq\psi(V_0)$ of $\varphi(p)$ and $\psi(F(p))$, the restriction $f|\widetilde U:\widetilde U\to \widetilde V$ is a bijection with $C^1$ inverse. Since $f$ is smooth, [L3] upgrades that inverse to a smooth one. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2, L3]

scientific_rationale: The published Statement admits zero-dimensional manifolds. Their tangent spaces are zero-dimensional; an invertible differential forces equal source/target dimensions. At dimension0, charts have singleton images and give open singleton domains, and the inverse singleton map is smooth by the actual local smoothness convention. Only the positive-dimensional branch invokes Euclidean IFT and its regularity bootstrap. Compatible charts are explicitly selected so the coordinate map has its displayed domain.
